title: Jump Operators, Interactive Proofs and Proof Complexity Generators
authors: Erfan Khaniki (University of Oxford, United Kingdom)
abstract: A jump operator J in proof complexity is a function such that for any proof system P, J(P) is a proof system that P cannot simulate. Some candidate jump operators were proposed by Krajíček and Pudlák [JSL, 1989] and Krajíček [JSL, 2004], but it is an open problem whether computable jump operators exist or not. In this regard, we introduce a new candidate jump operator based on the power of interactive proofs which given a proof system P, [[IP, P]] (IP-randomized implicit proof system based on P) is an MA proof system. In the first step, we investigate the relationship between IP-randomized implicit proof systems and Cook-Reckhow proof systems. In particular, we show that if iEF (Krajíček's implicit Extended Frege) proves exponential hard on average circuit lower bounds efficiently, then iEF simulates [[IP, EF]]. Moreover, we show that IP-randomized implicit proof systems can be used to prove new connections between different well-studied concepts in complexity theory. Namely, we prove new results about the hardness magnification in proof complexity, the hardness of proving proof complexity lower bounds, the automatability and the feasible disjunction property for Extended Frege using IP-randomized implicit proof systems. One ingredient of our proofs is a formalization of the sum-check protocol in S^1_2 which might be of independent interest. We also look at the general theory of jump operators and consider an old conjecture by Pudlák [Stud. Logic Found. Math., 1986] about finite consistency sentences for first-order theories of arithmetic. In this direction, we prove that certain statements are equivalent, in particular, we prove that the widely believed assumption about the existence of computable jump operators in proof complexity is equivalent to a weaker form of Pudlák's conjecture.

A long-standing problem in complexity theory is to prove
super-polynomial size lower bounds for any proof system
for propositional tautologies. This is closely related to the
well-known question NP vs. CoNP (see [21]). Although
there is a huge amount of work understanding the power
of proof systems (see [60]), the current techniques are not
strong enough to help us to prove lower bounds for strong
proof systems such as Extended Frege (EF). Apart from the
problem regarding the lack of good techniques to prove lower
bounds, there is also a lack of families of tautologies that
are believed to be hard for a proof system such as EF.

Another motivation behind the definition of IP-randomized
implicit proof systems is a generic way to define IPS like proof
systems based on an arbitrary proof system. Roughly speaking,
a proof in the Ideal proof system (IPS) of Grochow and Pitassi
[30] is an algebraic circuit that encodes a Nullstellensatz proof
of the unsatisfiability of a set of polynomials succinctly. Such
a clean and direct definition is possible for Nullstellensatz
because of the way it works, but it is not possible to directly
define IPS like proof systems for other proof systems such as
EF. IP-randomized proof systems give us a generic way to do
this for any proof system (another way of defining IPS like
proof systems is defined in Section VII based on another jump
operator that uses the PCP theorem).

It is well-known that EF is not automatable under some

not known whether we can prove the nonautomatability of

like the nonautomatability results for weak proof systems

(for another attempt for proving nonautomatability of strong

Another concept that is related to automatability is the feasible

nonautomatbility result for EF, we show that EF does not
have the feasible disjunction property under another structural
hardness assumption.
